newsitem.title: GERMANY: F.O. LICHT - Daily sugar report.
newsitem.headline: F.O. LICHT - Daily sugar report.

text.p: The following is a direct contribution from statistician F.O. Licht in Ratzeburg, Germany. Please address any queries to Helmut Ahlfeld on +00 49 4541 88920.

White sugar futures in London remained quiet with prices fluctuating in a narrow range. December ended $0.70 higher at $317.40. The March/May spread attracted some interest but otherwise activity was dull.
In New York raw sugar futures ended unchanged to lower with spot March losing 4 points to close at 10.7 cents/lb. May gave up 1 point to close at 10.71 cents/lb.

There are increasing signs that there will be a noticeable surplus this year. The Indian Sugar Mills Association indicated that production in 1996/97 may be significantly higher than estimated by international analysts, while Poland is likely to have a record crop. It remains to be seen whether this will have a negative impact on prices on Monday.

INDIA - The Indian Sugar Mills Association said that production in 1996/97 could reach more than 17 million tonnes in raw value terms, which compares to our recent estimate of 16.750 million tonnes and Man's figure of 16.033 million tonnes. Last year's production was put at 17.8 million tonnes.

However, Indian production is notoriously difficult to asses, so that significant changes later in the year cannot be excluded. The country has accumulated significant surplus stocks and is therefore keen to export more sugar. Commerce Minister B.B. Ramaiah recently said that the government is likely to take a decision soon on allowing fresh 500,000 tonnes of sugar for export in 1996/97.

In June the government had already authorized the export of one million tonnes. However, industry sources become wary about exporting sugar as currently the projected loss on the export of one tonne of sugar is around $40. On the other hand, carrying stocks is also an expensive operation, so that it cannot be totally excluded that India will export more.

One major market for Indian sugar is Pakistan, and the Indian Sugar Mills Association is confident that that country will take 500,000 tonnes of Indian sugar, due to a domestic production shortfall in 1996/97. The Association said that Pakistan is faced with a shortage of around 700,000 tonnes.

POLAND - According to the Polish Sugar Council sugar production in 1996/97 is forecast to rise to over 2.1 million tonnes, white value, up from 2 million tonnes estimated earlier and last year's production of 1.58 million tonnes. This means that the country would have a significant surplus this year, which may be difficult to export.

BRAZIL - Brazil exported 691,100 tonnes of sugar, raw value, in September 1996, down from 705,900 tonnes exported the previous month and down on the 755,300 tonnes exported the same month the previous year. That brought total exports since the beginning of 1996/97 (May/April) up to 2.622 million tonnes, nearly 16 per cent less than was exported the same period in 1995. Total exports in crop year 1995/96 reached 5.922 million tonnes, up from 4.352 million tonnes exported the previous year.

The main destination for raw sugar in May/September 1996 remained the United States with 123,012 tonnes, up from 26,855 tonnes the same period in 1995. In contrast to last year no raw sugar was exported to Russia.
Main white sugar destinations were Romania (156,826 vs 20,951 tonnes), Russia (152,186 vs 364,682 tonnes), Nigeria (311,925 vs 173,950 tonnes) and the Philippines (166,482 vs 0 tonnes).
